claims.claim: Propaganda is a form of communication intended to influence an audience to further an agenda; it may not be objective, often presents facts selectively, and can use loaded language to produce an emotional rather than a rational response.

The English word 'propaganda' derives from Modern Latin, the gerundive of propagare (to spread); its earliest institutional use was the Catholic Church's Congregatio de Propaganda Fide (Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith), created in 1622; from the 1790s the word also described secular activities, and its modern manipulative sense developed in the twentieth century.

The Institute for Propaganda Analysis (1937-1942), founded by Kirtley Mather, Edward A. Filene, and Clyde R. Miller, aimed to teach the public how to think rather than what to think and catalogued seven propaganda devices: name-calling, glittering generalities, transfer, testimonial, plain folks, card stacking, and bandwagon.

Additional documented techniques include loaded language (words with strong emotional implications), fear-based appeals (threats or doubts used to influence perception or push action), and repetition (repeating a symbol or slogan so the audience remembers it).

During World War I the poster became one of the most important means of communication: the Library of Congress collection includes approximately 1,900 posters created between 1914 and 1920 and used to inspire, inform, and persuade audiences, covering recruiting, war loans, and Red Cross appeals, and museum scholarship documents the period's printed propaganda and its distribution.

During World War II the U.S. government ran an organized persuasion campaign with clearly articulated goals and strategies, recruiting intellectuals, artists, and filmmakers; documented posters include 'I Want You' by James Montgomery Flagg (Army Recruiting Bureau version, 1940) and 'We Can Do It!' by J. Howard Miller, produced by Westinghouse for the War Production Co-Ordinating Committee; other governments operated official wartime information agencies (Germany's propaganda ministry, Britain's Political Warfare Executive, the U.S. Office of War Information).

Recognizing propaganda involves asking who benefits, what information is omitted, whether emotion replaces evidence, and whether the message is one-sided; the Institute for Propaganda Analysis' recognition-oriented purpose grounds this as an analytical and defensive practice, not a creative one.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Scope of the term: some scholarship treats commercial advertising as a type of propaganda, while other definitions restrict propaganda to political or ideological persuasion.
positions: Broad definitions treat any systematic persuasion, including advertising, as propaganda
Narrow definitions limit propaganda to political or ideological ends
conflictingEvidence.resolution: This lesson follows the narrower political/ideological definition, flags the existence of broader definitions, and keeps advertising as a sibling topic.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Dating of the 'I Want You' poster.
positions: The National Archives exhibit labels its copy 'I Want You' by James Montgomery Flagg, 1940 (Army Recruiting Bureau)
The design is widely attributed to 1917, during World War I
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson describes the NARA-documented 1940 Army Recruiting Bureau version and makes no claim about a 1917 origin.

sourceRecords.title: Propaganda techniques
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports the documented technique descriptions used in the lesson: loaded language (words and phrases with strong emotional implications chosen to influence the audience), repetition (repeating a symbol or slogan so the audience remembers it), bandwagon (urging the audience to take the course of action everyone else is taking), and fear/uncertainty-based appeals (FUD-style attempts to influence perception by disseminating negative or doubtful information). Facts synthesized; the lesson's examples are invented.
